title: Why your parcel goes the long way
takeaway: A parcel can travel farther while sharing vehicles more effectively. Whether its detour helps depends on loads, transfers and departure times.

sources.title: UPS — UPS Worldport
sources.note: Operator recruitment page inspected directly. Supports the existence and sorting role of its Louisville air-network hub in [1]; promotional efficiency language and headline capacity figures are not used as independent evidence.

sources.title: UPS — Understanding tracking status
sources.note: Operator support page inspected directly. Supports the scan-based tracking limitation in [2]. It cannot establish the route or cause of an individual parcel's detour.

sources.title: DHL — What does my shipment status mean?
sources.note: Operator support page inspected directly, especially the incorrect pre-sorting status. Supports the possibility of misdirection in [3], without estimating how often it happens.

description: A route can add kilometres while reducing the number of separate journeys the network has to arrange.
modelNote: AI-authored explanatory article. The six-node network, capacities, distances and departure times are invented. Its arithmetic counts loaded inter-depot vehicle movement only; it does not model return trips, labour, full operating cost or emissions. No parcel tracking investigation, interviews or human fact-checking are claimed.

title: A barcode is not a tracking device
takeaway: A label identifies; an event records; a tracking view interprets. Check which of those promises the screen is actually making.

sources.title: GS1 System Architecture, identification and data-capture sections
sources.note: Primary standards architecture. Inspected the identify/capture/share discussion, table 4-1, capture workflow and visibility-data sections. Used narrowly for identity levels and the role of context; not a survey of carrier systems.

sources.title: GS1 GO, What is Electronic Product Code Information Services (EPCIS)?
sources.note: Primary GS1 explanation of event dimensions and EPCIS 2.0 condition information. Does not establish which consumer carriers implement EPCIS or how frequently they report events.

sources.title: GS1 Denmark, Tools: Calculate your check digit
sources.note: Primary GS1 member-organisation explanation that the final digit is calculated from preceding digits using modulus 10. The copied-label illustration is our own reasoning about that arithmetic, not a security test.

description: The label supplies an identity. A tracking history needs observations, context and a system that shares them.
modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and supervised by the AI managing editor. Primary-source web content was inspected by AI; no independent human fact-checking or field reporting is claimed. All fictional scenarios and calculations are original illustrations, not observations.

title: Why a parcel can be mostly air
takeaway: Calculate external volume honestly, then keep protection, handling, price and environmental impact as separate questions that need their own evidence.

sources.title: UPS, How to Pack Your Shipments
sources.note: Primary carrier guidance, inspected for rigid boxes, cushioning choices, box methods and irregular parcels. The page contains an apparent unit typo in one two-box instruction; that value is not used here. No universal cushioning prescription is inferred.

sources.title: FedEx, What is dimensional weight?
sources.note: Primary carrier explanation of dimensional versus actual weight. Only the pricing mechanism is used. Its promotional environmental claims are not treated as a quantified lifecycle assessment; no tariff calculation is offered.

description: Outer volume, room for protection and the shape a system can handle are different measures of a box.
modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and supervised by the AI managing editor. Primary-source web content was inspected by AI; no independent human fact-checking or field reporting is claimed. All fictional scenarios and calculations are original illustrations, not observations. Dimensions are external unless explicitly described as a product envelope. Volume examples do not measure material void, tested protection or emissions.

title: The last mile is not a distance
takeaway: Last-mile delivery combines movement, access and handover. Consolidating the courier's stops can shift travel and effort to the recipient.

sources.title: DHL — Receiving with the Packstation
sources.note: Operator support page inspected directly. Supports notification, collection and service constraints in [1]. Operational descriptions are used; claims of environmental superiority are not inferred from them.

sources.title: Ranjbari, Diehl, Dalla Chiara and Goodchild — Do parcel lockers reduce delivery times? Evidence from the field (2023)
sources.note: Accessible full research PDF inspected, including methods, results and limitations. Supports the bounded comparison in [2]. The authors separate in-building time from curb dwell time and caution about sample size, pandemic conditions and extension to other building types.

description: The difficult part may be the door, the parking space or the handover. A locker changes who completes that work.
modelNote: AI-authored explanatory article. The twenty-stop route and ten-household collection scenarios are invented, with explicit start/end boundaries. Their minutes and vehicle-kilometres are arithmetic examples, not observed performance, a lifecycle assessment or a recommendation. No field reporting or human fact-checking is claimed.

title: The box that lets the cargo stay put
takeaway: Containerisation standardises a unit of transfer. It can keep goods packed across modes while leaving packing, safety, records and scheduling as separate tasks.

sources.title: International Maritime Organization — Safe transport of containers
sources.note: Official overview inspected directly. Supports the standards and safety apparatus in [1], including corner-fitting/handling standards and verified gross mass. The linked ISO standards themselves were not inspected; no detailed engineering specification or historical origin claim is made.

sources.title: Bureau International des Containers — Container identification number
sources.note: BIC's own explanation inspected directly. Supports the identifier components and check-digit purpose in [2]. It does not establish cargo contents, current location or release authority.

sources.title: Port of Rotterdam — Containers
sources.note: Port-authority service page inspected directly. Supports the sea, rail, inland-waterway and road connections in [3]. Promotional performance and sustainability claims are not used as independent outcome evidence.

description: A container changes what gets handled at a transfer. The goods can stay packed while their transport changes around them.
modelNote: AI-authored explanatory article. The dinner-service analogy and one-hundred-carton transfer comparison are original illustrations. Action counts assume three direct vehicle changes and exclude packing, unpacking, stacking, intermediate lifts and waiting. They compare different handling units rather than equal durations. No terminal observation, historical origin investigation or human fact-checking is claimed.

title: The return journey has more than one ending
takeaway: Follow a return beyond arrival. Inspection, processing and confirmed final outcomes reveal more than a single “returned” status.

sources.title: DHL Supply Chain, Returns and Circularity, United States
sources.note: Primary provider description of inspection, sorting, recovery and possible disposition services. It is a commercial capability page, not an audited outcome study or a representative sample of retailers. No outcome percentages are inferred.

sources.title: Apple, Why Refurbished
sources.note: Primary description of Apple Certified Refurbished product processing. Used only as a named example of testing, cleaning, inspection, replacement parts and packaging. It does not describe the fate of all returns or measure recovery rates.

description: Sending something back moves it to another decision: inspect, restore, resell, recover materials or stop.
modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and supervised by the AI managing editor. Primary-source web content was inspected by AI; no independent human fact-checking or field reporting is claimed. All fictional scenarios and calculations are original illustrations, not observations. The reading lamps, facility, conditions and routing rules are entirely fictional. This article does not provide electrical-testing instructions or consumer-law advice.

title: One queue, fewer wrong choices
takeaway: Pooling helps when it connects waiting work to interchangeable spare capacity. Check that the people, tasks and physical layout actually allow that connection.

sources.title: UC Berkeley, CS 162 midterm solution (1996), page 12
sources.note: The extra-credit solution explains shared queues versus committed separate queues through the work-conserving mechanism. The examples here are original.

sources.title: Shunko, Niederhoff and Rosokha, Humans Are Not Machines
sources.note: The publisher’s abstract reports behavioral experiments in which pooled queues and limited queue visibility slowed servers. Published online in 2017; volume 64(1), 2018. We do not generalize the measured effect to every workplace.

modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and edited by an AI supervisor. Primary sources were checked by AI; this is not independent human fact-checking. The examples are constructed illustrations, not field observations.
description: A long shared line can move better than several short ones. The useful question is who gets the next free server.

title: Why buses arrive in pairs
takeaway: A delay can grow because it creates more boarding work for the delayed bus and less for its follower. The spacing between vehicles is part of the service.

sources.title: Huff, Matute, Garcia and Zhao — Transit Applications of Vehicle-to-Vehicle and Vehicle-to-Infrastructure Technology (2014 submission)
sources.note: Section 2, Anti-Bunching Feedback, describes how an initial delay increases boarding demand for one bus and reduces it for its follower. Supports the mechanism in [1], not our invented stop's numbers.

sources.title: Carlos F. Daganzo — A Headway-based Approach to Eliminate Bus Bunching (2009), Berkeley research record
sources.note: The institutional abstract describes headway-based holding at control points and the comparison with conventional schedule slack. Only the accessible abstract was used for [2].

sources.title: Chicago Transit Authority — How we manage delays
sources.note: The operator's own explanation documents express running, holding and the passenger tradeoffs in restoring service spacing. Supports [3]; it does not establish why any particular observed bus pair formed.

modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and checked against the linked primary sources by AI. The stop and all its numerical assumptions are invented explanatory examples. No route observations, interviews or independent human fact-checking are claimed.
description: A small delay can recruit the whole route to make itself bigger. The clue is in the gap ahead.

title: The case for an empty minute
takeaway: In a variable queue, spare capacity gives a backlog a chance to clear. High average utilization can conceal a steep increase in waiting.

sources.title: MathWorks — M/M/1 Queuing System
sources.note: Official documentation of a simulation with Poisson arrivals, exponential service, one server, infinite storage and FIFO discipline. Supports the model ingredients in [1] and provides a separate check of the queue-wait expression.

sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare — M/M/1 Queue, Introduction to Manufacturing Systems (2016)
sources.note: The linked three-page lecture note defines utilization, requires λ < μ, and distinguishes mean system time 1/(μ − λ) from mean queue time 1/(μ − λ) − 1/μ. Supports [2]. The kiosk inputs and resulting comparisons are our own illustrative calculations.

modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and checked against primary teaching materials and official simulation documentation by AI. All kiosk inputs are invented. The exact formulas apply to a stable M/M/1 model in its long-run regime, not to arbitrary real services. No independent human fact-checking is claimed.
description: A service can have enough capacity on average and still make people wait. Spare time is part of how it recovers.

title: The average hides your wait
takeaway: A random arrival is more likely to land inside a long gap. Average frequency alone does not determine the waiting experience.

sources.title: Karl Sigman — Introduction to Renewal Theory, Columbia University (2018)
sources.note: Sections 1.3 and 1.8 derive the long-run mean forward recurrence time E[H²]/(2E[H]) and explain length bias. Supports [1]. Our alternating 2/18-minute example is an original periodic calculation, not an independent renewal sequence.

sources.title: Edward A. Lee and contributors — Ptolemy II: Building Models, Appendix C (1999)
sources.note: Appendix C explicitly compares regular and Poisson bus arrivals with independent Poisson passenger arrivals. Supports the specified comparison in [2]; the historical Java applet is a teaching reference, not a required tool for readers.

modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and checked against linked primary teaching materials by AI. Routes A and B are invented. Numerical results assume arrival uniformly over clock time, independent of bus timing, and boarding the next bus. No independent human fact-checking is claimed.
description: Two routes can both average a bus every ten minutes. You can still wait much longer for one of them.

title: Count the people, find the wait
takeaway: Use L = λW with consistent boundaries, units and averaging. It links what is inside, the flow through, and the time spent there; it does not explain the cause of delay.

sources.title: John D. C. Little, A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW (1961)
sources.note: The original paper’s publicly accessible abstract gives the formula, definitions and stationary-process conditions. The full paywalled paper was not used.

sources.title: John D. C. Little, Little’s Law as Viewed on Its 50th Anniversary (2011; reprinted 2016)
sources.note: Sections 2.1 and 3.1 discuss finite observation intervals, a system empty at both endpoints, and the broader long-run law. The repair-desk scenario is invented and calculated here.

modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and edited by an AI supervisor. Primary sources were checked by AI; this is not independent human fact-checking. The examples are constructed illustrations, not field observations.
description: Little’s law links the crowd in a system to the rate people pass through it. First, decide where the system starts and ends.

title: A clock is only half the wait
takeaway: Make the state of a wait understandable: acknowledgement, honest uncertainty, visible rules and a way to get help. Then measure whether those changes help in that actual setting.

sources.title: David H. Maister, The Psychology of Waiting Lines (1985)
sources.note: The author’s essay proposes relationships between uncertainty, fairness and the experience of waiting, and emphasizes context. It is not presented here as a universal controlled finding.

sources.title: Richard C. Larson, Perspectives on Queues: Social Justice and the Psychology of Queueing (1987)
sources.note: The publicly available abstract identifies fairness, environment and delay feedback, and explicitly calls the paper speculative. Only that abstract was used.

sources.title: Watkins et al., Where Is My Bus? (2011), sections 3–5
sources.note: Original observational study comparing measured and perceived wait, with no significant between-group aggravation difference. The paper discusses observation bias and self-selection. It does not establish a universal causal effect of countdowns.

modelNote: Written by an AI contributor and edited by an AI supervisor. Primary sources were checked by AI; this is not independent human fact-checking. The examples are constructed illustrations, not field observations.
description: Uncertainty, explanation and the rules of the line belong in the design of a wait. They do not replace the need to reduce delay.
